meta.description: Not Hemingway. The line began as fictional dialogue by car writer Ken Purdy in his 1957 story “Blood Sport” — and the popular wording paraphrases even that.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are only three sports: bullfighting, motor racing, and mountaineering; all the rest are merely games'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Hemingway. It began as fictional dialogue by automotive writer Ken Purdy in 1957 — and the famous wording paraphrases even his original line.

answer.label: Not Ernest Hemingway — actually Ken Purdy (and paraphrased)
answer.authorDates: Kenneth William Purdy · 1913–1972 · American automotive writer & editor
answer.sourceLine: The line is not found anywhere in Hemingway. It began as fictional dialogue written by automotive journalist Ken Purdy in his short story “Blood Sport” (The Saturday Evening Post, 27 July 1957), spoken by a Hemingway-modelled character — and Purdy’s wording was “bullfighting, motor racing, mountain climbing… all the rest are recreations,” so the familiar “merely games” version paraphrases even the real source.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from
source.excerpt: There are only three sports: bullfighting, motor racing, and mountaineering; all the rest are merely games.
trail: Etymologist Barry Popik traces the line to Ken Purdy’s story “Blood Sport,” where it is spoken by the character Helmut Ovden — a figure modelled on Hemingway, which likely seeded the misattribution.

Purdy later recounted floating the idea to racing driver Alfonso de Portago in his 1960 book The Wonderful World of the Automobile; by a 1976 book it was even called “the Marquis de Portago’s dictum,” per Popik.
Motorsport writer Elizabeth Blackstock reaches the same conclusion, noting the phrase “is not actually a Hemingway quote” but a Purdy invention, in her debunking of the quote.
source.cutTag: Attributed to Hemingway only from the late 1980s
source.excerptNote: This is the modern popular form. Ken Purdy’s original 1957 dialogue reads differently — his character names “bullfighting, motor racing, mountain climbing” and calls the rest “recreations,” per Barry Popik’s citation history.

sourceLink.text: Barry Popik: full citation history of the ‘three sports’ line

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording (“merely games”) is a later paraphrase found in no identifiable published work, so no clean rights status can be asserted. Its nearest documented source — Ken Purdy’s 1957 story “Blood Sport” — is itself firmly in copyright (first published 1957), so the line is certainly not public domain.

author.name: Ken Purdy
author.heading: Who was Ken Purdy?
author.bio: Kenneth William Purdy (1913–1972) was one of the most admired American automotive journalists of the mid-20th century, an editor at magazines including Parade, True and Argosy and author of the landmark motoring book Kings of the Road. He also wrote fiction, and it was in his 1957 short story “Blood Sport” that a race-driver character — modelled on Hemingway — first delivered the ‘three sports’ line. The motorsport press’s Ken Purdy Award for excellence is named in his honour.

cite.sourceCitation: Ken Purdy, “Blood Sport,” The Saturday Evening Post, 27 July 1957 (line spoken by the character Helmut Ovden); citation history documented by Barry Popik, “Auto Racing, Bullfighting, and Mountain Climbing Are the Only Real Sports.”

copyAttribution: Misattributed to Ernest Hemingway. The line actually originates as fictional dialogue in Ken Purdy's short story "Blood Sport" (The Saturday Evening Post, 27 July 1957); Purdy's original said "recreations," not "merely games." Documented by Barry Popik.

misattribution.heading: How Hemingway got the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is a magnet for famous names. It has been pinned on at least three men — and the one it fits worst, textually, is the one it’s now most often given to.

items.why: The line appears in none of Hemingway’s bullfighting works — not Death in the Afternoon (1932), his 1960 Life articles, nor The Dangerous Summer (1985). The likely seed: Purdy’s fictional speaker Helmut Ovden was modelled on Hemingway. The earliest documented Hemingway attribution is a 1988 newspaper column, decades after Purdy wrote it, per Barry Popik.
The Spanish racing aristocrat was credited with the line as the “Marquis de Portago’s dictum” — but Purdy’s own account has him proposing the idea to Portago, who merely agreed, per Popik.

The bullfighter-author of Matador (1952) is sometimes named, another famous bullfighting figure who fits the sentiment but did not originate the wording — and, as Barry Popik notes, there is no documentary evidence for the Conrad credit.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is Ken Purdy, who put the thought in a fictional character’s mouth in 1957 — and even he said “recreations,” not “merely games,” per Barry Popik’s citation record.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: The quote fuses three high-stakes pursuits Hemingway genuinely loved to write about — bullfighting above all — with a terse, declarative cadence that sounds like him. That resemblance is not a coincidence: Ken Purdy built his fictional speaker as a Hemingway type, so the line was Hemingway-flavoured from birth.

Strip away the famous name and it is a piece of romantic mid-century motorsport writing, produced at the height of a deadly era in Grand Prix racing — de Portago himself was killed at the 1957 Mille Miglia, weeks before “Blood Sport” ran.
detailsBody: Purdy’s 1957 line: “bullfighting, motor racing, mountain climbing… all the rest are recreations.”

Popular modern form: “bullfighting, motor racing, and mountaineering; all the rest are merely games.” The swap of “recreations” for “merely games” and “mountain climbing” for “mountaineering” are the tell-tale marks of a paraphrase that hardened over decades of repetition.
context.pull: A Hemingway-shaped character said it first — so the world gave it to Hemingway.
